claim: CaMKII has a unique architecture in which the catalytic domains are linked flexibly to a hub domain that forms a dodecameric or tetradecameric assembly.
source: CaMKII has a unique architecture, in which the catalytic domains are linked flexibly to a hub domain, also called the association domain, which forms a dodecameric or tetradecameric assembly (see Figure 1A for a description of the domains of CaMKII) (Chao et al., 2011; Kanaseki et al., 1991; Kolb et al., 1998; Kolodziej et al., 2000; Morris and Török, 2001; Rosenberg et al., 2006; Stratton et al., 2013; Woodgett et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A

claim: The organization of CaMKII, with twelve or more kinase domains maintained in close proximity, enables highly cooperative activation by Ca2+/calmodulin and integration of calcium inputs.
source: This organization, in which twelve or more kinase domains are maintained in close proximity, enables the highly cooperative activation of CaMKII by Ca2+/calmodulin (Ca2+/CaM) and the integration of calcium inputs (Bradshaw et al., 2003; Chao et al., 2010, 2011; De Koninck and Schulman, 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The activation loop of the CaMKII kinase domain has no phosphorylation site and is in an active conformation.
source: The activation loop of the CaMKII kinase domain has no phosphorylation site, and is in an active conformation (Bulleit et al., 1988; Hanley et al., 1987; Lin et al., 1987; Rosenberg et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The three principal sites of autophosphorylation in CaMKII are located within the autoinhibitory segment.
source: The three principal sites of autophosphorylation in CaMKII are located within the autoinhibitory segment, which follows the N-terminal kinase domain and blocks the catalytic site in the unactivated state of the enzyme (Figure 1).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 prevents rebinding of the autoinhibitory segment to the kinase domain and is the key step by which CaMKII gains calcium-independence after stimulation by Ca2+/CaM.
source: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 is the key step by which CaMKII gains calcium-independence (autonomy) after stimulation by Ca2+/CaM (Colbran et al., 1989b; Lou and Schulman, 1989; Miller et al., 1988; Schworer et al., 1988; Thiel et al., 1988; Waldmann et al., 1990) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: Thr 305 and Thr 306 are located within an 18 residue CaM-binding element that is part of the autoinhibitory segment.
source: The other two sites, Thr 305 and Thr 306, are located within an 18 residue CaM-binding element that is part of the autoinhibitory segment (Figure 1B) (Meador et al., 1993; Rellos et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr 305 and Thr 306 prevents the rebinding of Ca2+/CaM to CaMKII.
source: Phosphorylation of these two sites prevents the rebinding of Ca2+/CaM to CaMKII (Elgersma et al., 2002; Hanson et al., 1994; Hashimoto et al., 1987; Lickteig et al., 1988; Lou and Schulman, 1989; Mukherji and Soderling, 1994).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Mice in which Thr 286, Thr 305, and Thr 306 are mutated exhibit distinct defects in learning and memory.
source: The importance of phosphorylation at these three sites is underscored by the fact that mice in which these sites are mutated exhibit distinct defects in learning and memory (Elgersma et al., 2002; Giese et al., 1998; Silva et al., 1992; Wayman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Activation of CaMKII-α by ATP and Ca2+/CaM triggers the exchange of activated subunits between different holoenzyme assemblies.
source: We reported recently that the activation of CaMKII-α by ATP and Ca2+/CaM triggers the exchange of activated subunits between different holoenzyme assemblies (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Replacement of Thr 286 by aspartate results in robust subunit exchange without Ca2+/CaM and the spread of activation to unactivated subunits.
source: The replacement of Thr 286 by aspartate, which confers constitutive activity on the kinase (Waldmann et al., 1990), results in robust subunit exchange without Ca2+/CaM, and the spread of activation to unactivated subunits.
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The β isoform of CaMKII undergoes activation-dependent subunit exchange.
source: We show that the β isoform also undergoes activation-dependent subunit exchange.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the abstract

claim: The intact human CaMKII-α holoenzyme exists as a mixture of dodecameric and tetradecameric forms.
source: We show that the intact human CaMKII-α holoenzyme exists as a mixture of dodecameric and tetradecameric forms, an observation that provides a link to a possible mechanism for subunit exchange.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the abstract

claim: The CaM-binding element of CaMKII can bind to the hub of the holoenzyme and destabilize it to release dimers.
source: We show that the intact human CaMKII-α holoenzyme exists as a mixture of dodecameric and tetradecameric forms, an observation that provides a link to a possible mechanism for subunit exchange. We demonstrate that the CaM-binding element of CaMKII is subject to a three-way competition for binding, between the kinase domain, Ca2+/CaM and the hub.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the abstract

claim: The CaM-binding element of activated CaMKII acts as a wedge by docking at intersubunit interfaces in the hub, converting the hub into a spiral form that can release or gain CaMKII dimers.
source: The structures of CaMKII from two distantly diverged organisms suggest that the CaM-binding element of activated CaMKII acts as a wedge by docking at intersubunit interfaces in the hub. This converts the hub into a spiral form that can release or gain CaMKII dimers.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the abstract based on structural data

claim: Phosphorylation biases the CaM-binding element towards the hub interface, away from the kinase domain and calmodulin, unlocking the ability of activated CaMKII holoenzymes to exchange dimers with unactivated ones.
source: Our data reveal a three-way competition for the CaM-binding element, whereby phosphorylation biases it towards the hub interface, away from the kinase domain and calmodulin, thus unlocking the ability of activated CaMKII holoenzymes to exchange dimers with unactivated ones.
evidence: Stated as a finding in the abstract

claim: The isolated hub assembly of human CaMKII-α exists as a ~1:1 mixture of dodecamers and tetradecamers in solution.
source: The mass spectra demonstrate that the isolated hub assembly exists as a ~1:1 mixture of dodecamers and tetradecamers in solution.
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS data

claim: Collision-induced dissociation MS/MS of the hub parent ions shows the presence of fragment ions corresponding to a hub monomer and a mixture of 11-subunit and 13-subunit species.
source: Collision-induced dissociation (CID) MS/MS of the mixture of hub parent ions (at 30 V collision energy) shows the presence of fragment ions corresponding to a hub monomer and a mixture of 11-subunit and 13-subunit species (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by CID MS/MS data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The crystal structures of dodecameric and tetradecameric hubs are not artifacts of crystallization, but reflect a natural variation in the stoichiometry of assembly of the hub.
source: This validates the mixed stoichiometry of the parent ion. Thus, the crystal structures of dodecameric and tetradecameric hubs are not artifacts of crystallization, but reflect instead a natural variation in the stoichiometry of assembly of the hub.
evidence: Inferred from MS/MS data validating mixed stoichiometry

claim: Negative-stain electron microscopy of unactivated human CaMKII-α holoenzyme reveals a population of holoenzyme particles with seven-fold symmetry, in addition to those with six-fold symmetry.
source: Visual inspection of the two-dimensional class averages clearly reveals a population of holoenzyme particles with seven-fold symmetry, in addition to those with the expected six-fold symmetry.
evidence: Demonstrated by negative-stain EM analysis

claim: The ratio of dodecameric to tetradecameric species in full-length human CaMKII-α is roughly 55:45.
source: Based on the number of particles contributing to each of these 14 classes, we estimate the ratio of dodecameric to tetradecameric species to be roughly 55:45 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Estimated from EM class averages shown in Figure 2B

claim: The dodecameric and tetradecameric species can interconvert by releasing and capturing dimers.
source: If CaMKII dimers are the unit of exchange, as we hypothesized previously, then the dodecameric and tetradecameric species can interconvert by releasing and capturing dimers (Figure 2C).
evidence: Proposed mechanism illustrated in Figure 2C

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 can only occur in trans.
source: Phosphorylation of Thr 286 can only occur in trans (Hanson et al., 1994; Rich and Schulman, 1998), and a dimeric unit may be able to maintain this phosphorylation whereas a monomer could not.
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Mutation of the CaM-binding element blocks subunit exchange.
source: We had shown previously that mutation of the CaM-binding element blocks subunit exchange, and that phosphorylation of Thr 305 and Thr 306 in the CaM-binding element potentiates exchange (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr 305 and Thr 306 in the CaM-binding element potentiates subunit exchange.
source: We had shown previously that mutation of the CaM-binding element blocks subunit exchange, and that phosphorylation of Thr 305 and Thr 306 in the CaM-binding element potentiates exchange (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for the unphosphorylated CaM-binding element peptide binding to the hub is approximately 90 μM.
source: The values of the corresponding dissociation constants (KD), derived from non-linear least squares fit of the data by assuming that each subunit has a single peptide-binding site, are ~90 μM, ~60 μM and ~50 μM, for the unphosphorylated peptide, and peptides phosphorylated on Thr 305 and Thr 306, respectively (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Derived from competition experiments and curve fitting

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for the peptide phosphorylated on Thr 305 binding to the hub is approximately 60 μM.
source: The values of the corresponding dissociation constants (KD), derived from non-linear least squares fit of the data by assuming that each subunit has a single peptide-binding site, are ~90 μM, ~60 μM and ~50 μM, for the unphosphorylated peptide, and peptides phosphorylated on Thr 305 and Thr 306, respectively (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Derived from competition experiments and curve fitting

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) for the peptide phosphorylated on Thr 306 binding to the hub is approximately 50 μM.
source: The values of the corresponding dissociation constants (KD), derived from non-linear least squares fit of the data by assuming that each subunit has a single peptide-binding site, are ~90 μM, ~60 μM and ~50 μM, for the unphosphorylated peptide, and peptides phosphorylated on Thr 305 and Thr 306, respectively (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Derived from competition experiments and curve fitting

claim: Phosphorylation of the CaM-binding element peptide at either Thr 305 or Thr 306, separately, does not alter the affinity for the hub substantially.
source: These data show that phosphorylation of the peptide at either Thr 305 or Thr 306, separately, does not alter the affinity for the hub substantially (see Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by competition experiments shown in Figure 3D-E

claim: The effective concentration of the CaM-binding element with respect to the hub in the intact holoenzyme is approximately 3 mM.
source: We estimated the local concentration of the CaM-binding element by assuming that the linker restricts it to within 50 Å of the hub. This corresponds to an effective concentration of ~3 mM (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Calculated based on geometric constraints shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The observed KD of ~100 μM would allow the CaM-binding element to successfully engage the hub in the holoenzyme.
source: Thus, the observed KD of ~100 μM would allow the CaM-binding element to successfully engage the hub in the holoenzyme.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of KD to effective concentration

claim: The unphosphorylated autoinhibitory segment binds to Ca2+/CaM with sub-picomolar affinity.
source: The unphosphorylated autoinhibitory segment, which includes the CaM-binding element, binds to Ca2+/CaM with sub-picomolar affinity (Tse et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Thr 305 and Thr 306 are buried within the high affinity interface between the autoinhibitory segment and Ca2+/CaM.
source: Thr 305 and Thr 306 are buried within this high affinity interface (Crivici and Ikura, 1995; Meador et al., 1992), and phosphorylation would therefore disrupt the interaction with Ca2+/CaM.
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr 305 and Thr 306 would disrupt the interaction between the autoinhibitory segment and Ca2+/CaM.
source: Thr 305 and Thr 306 are buried within this high affinity interface (Crivici and Ikura, 1995; Meador et al., 1992), and phosphorylation would therefore disrupt the interaction with Ca2+/CaM.
evidence: Inferred from structural information cited

claim: The autoinhibitory segment binds to the kinase domain and inhibits it with an IC50 value of ~1 μM when added in trans as a peptide.
source: The autoinhibitory segment also binds to the kinase domain, which it inhibits with an IC50 value of ~1 μM, when added in trans as a peptide (Colbran et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: Phosphorylation on Thr 286 increases the affinity of CaMKII for Ca2+/CaM by more than 1000-fold by fully or partially releasing the autoinhibitory segment from the kinase domain.
source: Phosphorylation on Thr 286 increases the affinity of CaMKII for Ca2+/CaM by more than 1000-fold, by fully or partially releasing the autoinhibitory segment from the kinase domain (Meyer et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The hub-△kinase construct (hub, linker, and autoinhibitory segment without kinase domain) undergoes robust subunit exchange.
source: We observed that the hub-△kinase construct undergoes robust subunit exchange (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 4A

claim: The isolated hub of CaMKII-α, lacking the autoinhibitory segment and the linker, does not exchange subunits.
source: In contrast, the isolated hub of CaMKII-α, lacking the autoinhibitory segment and the linker, does not exchange subunits (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Robust subunit exchange occurs only when the CaM-binding element is present in both samples.
source: We observe robust subunit exchange only when the CaM-binding element is present in both samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: A hub construct bearing the CaM-binding element cannot efficiently break a hub assembly lacking this element.
source: That is, a hub construct bearing the CaM-binding element cannot efficiently break a hub assembly lacking this element.
evidence: Inferred from FRET experiments

claim: The isolated hub shows one peak in analytical gel filtration, with a retention volume corresponding to dodecamer/tetradecamer.
source: The isolated hub shows one peak, with a retention volume corresponding to dodecamer/tetradecamer, as estimated from calibration data (see Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by analytical gel filtration shown in Figure 4B

claim: The hub-△kinase construct shows two peaks in analytical gel filtration, corresponding to dodecamer/tetradecamer and dimer.
source: The hub-△kinase construct shows two peaks, corresponding to dodecamer/tetradecamer and dimer, respectively.
evidence: Demonstrated by analytical gel filtration shown in Figure 4B

claim: For the hub-△kinase construct, approximately 65% of the sample corresponds to the dodecamer/tetradecamer and approximately 35% corresponds to a dimeric species.
source: The major peak (~65% of the sample) corresponds to the dodecamer/tetradecamer, and the minor peak (~35% of the sample) corresponds to a dimeric species.
evidence: Quantified from gel filtration data

claim: Reinjection of the eluate corresponding to the major peak of hub-△kinase results in two peaks at the same retention times as in the original experiment, suggesting an equilibrium between dodecamers/tetradecamers and dimers.
source: Reinjection of the eluate corresponding to the major peak results in two peaks at the same retention times as in the original experiment, suggesting that there is an equilibrium between dodecamers/tetradecamers and dimers (data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by reinjection experiment

claim: The CaMKII hub consists of two rings that are joined together at the equatorial plane.
source: The CaMKII hub consists of two rings that are joined together at the equatorial plane, each consisting of either six or seven subunits in dodecamers and tetradecamers, respectively.
evidence: Based on structural knowledge

claim: The upper and lower rings of the CaMKII hub do not separate readily.
source: Given that the upper and lower rings do not separate readily (Stratton et al., 2014), we sought to check whether the hub would release monomers or "vertical dimers", comprising one subunit each from the upper and lower rings (see Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: The F397A mutant hub exhibits a substantial release of dimers (~40% for the hub and ~60% for the holoenzyme).
source: Both the mutant hub and holoenzyme exhibited a substantial release of dimers (~40% for the hub and ~60% for the holoenzyme), even at an elevated injection concentration of 3–5 μM (Figure 4D).
evidence: Demonstrated by analytical gel filtration shown in Figure 4D

claim: Isolation and reinjection of the peak corresponding to the dodecamer/tetradecamer in the F397A holoenzyme resulted in further release of dimers, suggesting an equilibrium.
source: Isolation and reinjection of the peak corresponding to the dodecamer/tetradecamer in the holoenzyme resulted in further release of dimers, suggesting that there was an equilibrium (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by reinjection experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Mass spectrometry of the F397A mutant hub confirmed the presence of dimers.
source: Mass spectrometry of the F397A mutant hub confirmed the presence of dimers (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by mass spectrometry shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: Vertical dimers are the unit of assembly of the CaMKII hub, with each vertical dimer contributing one subunit each to the upper and lower rings.
source: This is consistent with vertical dimers being the unit of assembly of the CaMKII hub, with each vertical dimer contributing one subunit each to the upper and lower rings.
evidence: Inferred from F397A mutant data

claim: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β are the predominant species in the brain.
source: CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β are the predominant species in the brain (Tombes et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation

claim: The principal difference between CaMKII-α and CaMKII-β is the length of the linker, which is 218 residues long in CaMKII-β, compared to 30 residues in CaMKII-α.
source: The principal difference between these two isoforms is the length of the linker, which is 218 residues long in CaMKII-β, compared to 30 residues in CaMKII-α.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison

claim: CaMKII-β exchanges subunits only after stimulation with Ca2+/CaM and ATP.
source: This experiment shows that CaMKII-β exchanges subunits, but only after stimulation with Ca2+/CaM and ATP (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 5B

claim: The phenomenon of activation-triggered subunit exchange is not limited to just the α isoform of CaMKII.
source: Thus, the phenomenon of activation-triggered subunit exchange is not limited to just the α isoform of CaMKII (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 5B-C

claim: CaMKII-β can exchange subunits with CaMKII-α in an activation-dependent manner, leading to the formation of CaMKII heterooligomers.
source: CaMKII-β can also exchange subunits with CaMKII-α in an activation-dependent manner, leading to the formation of CaMKII heterooligomers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: In the crystal structure of human CaMKII-α hub, the N-terminal expression tag binds at two out of twelve intersubunit interfaces with well-resolved electron density.
source: To our surprise, we found well-resolved electron density corresponding to the expression tag at two out of the twelve intersubunit interfaces.
evidence: Observed in crystal structure

claim: The expression tag binds the hub by extending the central β-sheet of the hub domain by forming an additional parallel strand.
source: The tag binds the hub almost precisely as we had predicted the CaM-binding element would, and it extends the central β-sheet of the hub domain by forming an additional parallel strand (Figure 6A).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 6A

claim: The groove between adjacent subunits is narrower in the tetradecamer than in the dodecamer because of the hinging apart of the subunits.
source: The groove between adjacent subunits is necessarily narrower in the tetradecamer than in the dodecamer, because of the hinging apart of the subunits, and the presence of the expression tag could favor the dodecamer for this reason.
evidence: Inferred from structural comparison

claim: In the N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub structure at pH 4.2, a 12-residue segment of the linker is ordered in every subunit and folds back to dock onto the central β-sheet of the same hub subunit.
source: In the structure of the N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub at pH 4.2, this segment is ordered in every subunit, and it folds back to dock onto the central β-sheet of the same hub subunit, extending the β-sheet by one strand, as seen in the structure described earlier for human CaMKII-α (Figure 6B).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 6B

claim: The linker peptide cannot be accommodated within the grooves of the closed-ring forms without steric clashes.
source: Comparison of the N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub at pH 4.2 with that of tetradecameric or dodecameric hubs shows that the linker peptide cannot be accommodated within the grooves of the closed-ring forms without steric clashes.
evidence: Inferred from structural comparison

claim: The sidechain of Ile 335 in the N. vectensis docked linker would collide with Asp 393 in helix D in the adjacent subunit if the geometries of either the tetradecameric or dodecameric hubs were preserved.
source: In particular, the sidechain of Ile 335 in the N. vectensis docked linker would collide with the Asp 393 in helix D in the adjacent subunit if the geometries of either the tetradecameric or dodecameric hubs were preserved (Figure 6C).
evidence: Demonstrated by structural superposition shown in Figure 6C

claim: The N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub at pH 4.2 adopts a left-handed spiral geometry with a slight opening between the A-B and M-N dimers.
source: The assembly is distorted at each interface in a systematic way throughout. This leads to the formation of a spiral, similar to a "lock-washer", with a slight opening between the A-B and M-N dimers (subunit notation is indicated in Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 6D

claim: Apart from the rupture at the A-B/M-N interface, the rest of the CaMKII-B hub assembly is symmetrical.
source: Apart from the rupture at the A-B/M-N interface, the rest of the CaMKII-B hub assembly is symmetrical.
evidence: Observed in crystal structure

claim: At the interface between subunits B and N in the N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub, the sidechains of Gln 436, Thr 446 and Asn 411 are pulled away from their hydrogen bonding partners in the other subunit.
source: For example, at the interface between subunits B and N, the sidechains of Gln 436, Thr 446 and Asn 411 are pulled away from their hydrogen bonding partners in the other subunit.
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 7B

claim: Modeling of the RRKLK motif of the CaM-binding element docked onto a hub interface results in good electrostatic complementarity between the peptide sidechains and acidic sidechains in the hub.
source: We then altered the sequence of the peptide to an RRKLK motif that is present in the CaM-binding element. This results in good electrostatic complementarity between the peptide sidechains and acidic sidechains in the hub (Figure 7C).
evidence: Demonstrated by modeling shown in Figure 7C

claim: In molecular dynamics simulations of the tetradecameric hub with modeled CaM-binding element, a conformational change occurs at the interface that closely resembles the difference seen between the ring-opened N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub and the closed tetradecameric rings.
source: For the tetradecameric simulations (two independent trajectories, 100 ns each), a conformational change occurs at the interface in both trajectories (Figure 7D); no corresponding change was seen in the dodecamer in these relatively short trajectories. Remarkably, the structural change closely resembles the difference seen between the ring-opened N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub and the closed tetradecameric rings in N. vectensis CaMKII-A and mouse CaMKII-α.
evidence: Demonstrated by molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 7D

claim: Electrostatic complementarity between the CaM-binding element and the hub interface allows the docking of this element onto the hub.
source: Thus, we propose that electrostatic complementarity between the CaM-binding element and the hub interface allows the docking of this element onto the hub.
evidence: Proposed based on modeling and simulation data

claim: Engagement of the interface by the CaM-binding element results in a conformational change that favors a ring-opened "lock-washer" configuration of the assembly, rather than a closed ring.
source: Engagement of the interface by the CaM-binding element then results in a conformational change that favors a ring-opened "lock-washer" configuration of the assembly, rather than a closed ring.
evidence: Proposed based on structural and simulation data

claim: The choanoflagellate S. rosetta has one CaMKII gene.
source: The choanoflagellate S. rosetta has one CaMKII gene (Burkhardt et al., 2014; Fairclough et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations

claim: The S. rosetta CaMKII kinase domain is 52% identical in sequence to the corresponding domain of human CaMKII-α.
source: The S. rosetta kinase domain, including the autoinhibitory segment, and the hub are 52% and 41% identical in sequence to the corresponding domains of human CaMKII-α.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison

claim: The S. rosetta CaMKII hub is 41% identical in sequence to the hub of human CaMKII-α.
source: The S. rosetta kinase domain, including the autoinhibitory segment, and the hub are 52% and 41% identical in sequence to the corresponding domains of human CaMKII-α.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison

claim: S. rosetta CaMKII contains a residue equivalent to Thr 286 but lacks the two inhibitory phosphorylation sites within the CaM-binding element (Thr 305 and Thr 306).
source: Although S. rosetta CaMKII contains a residue that is equivalent to Thr 286, it lacks the two inhibitory phosphorylation sites within the CaM-binding element of the autoinhibitory segment (Thr 305 and Thr 306), as well as sites of regulatory glycosylation, nitrosylation and oxidation (Coultrap et al., 2014; Erickson et al., 2008, 2013, 2015).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison and citations

claim: The structure of the autoinhibited S. rosetta CaMKII kinase domain is very similar to that of autoinhibited human CaMKII-δ kinase domain.
source: The structure of the autoinhibited kinase domain was determined at 2.9 Å resolution, and is very similar to that of autoinhibited human CaMKII-δ kinase domain (Rellos et al., 2010) (PDB code: 2VN9; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: The S. rosetta CaMKII hub forms a vertical dimer that closely resembles those formed by the hubs of mammalian, C. elegans, and N. vectensis CaMKII proteins.
source: The S. rosetta CaMKII hub forms a vertical dimer that closely resembles those formed by the hubs of mammalian (PDB codes: 1HKX and 2UX0), the nematode C. elegans (Rosenberg et al., 2006) (PDB code: 2F86) and N. vectensis CaMKII proteins.
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison

claim: The mouse CaMKII-α hub dimer can be superimposed on the S. rosetta dimer with a rms deviation in Cα positions of 1.4 Å over 197 residues.
source: The mouse CaMKII-α hub dimer can be superimposed on the S. rosetta dimer with a rms deviation in Cα positions of 1.4 Å over 197 residues.
evidence: Calculated from structural superposition

claim: The quaternary assembly of the S. rosetta hub forms a right-handed spiral corresponding to a hexagonal P61 screw axis in the crystal lattice, instead of a closed ring.
source: The quaternary assembly of the S. rosetta hub is strikingly different from that of all other hubs in that it forms a right-handed spiral, corresponding to a hexagonal P61 screw axis in the crystal lattice, instead of a closed ring (Figure 8A).
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 8A

claim: The helical pitch of the S. rosetta hub assembly is such that the sixth dimer is displaced vertically by the length of a dimer with respect to the first one, positioning the seventh dimer directly above the first one.
source: An orthogonal view shows that the helical pitch of the assembly is such that the sixth dimer is displaced vertically by the length of a dimer, with respect to the first one (Figure 8A). This positions the seventh dimer directly above the first one.
evidence: Observed in crystal structure shown in Figure 8A

claim: At an injection concentration of 700 nM, full-length S. rosetta CaMKII forms a dimer as revealed by analytical gel filtration.
source: At an injection concentration of 700 nM, full-length S. rosetta CaMKII forms a dimer, as revealed by analytical gel filtration (Figure 8B).
evidence: Demonstrated by analytical gel filtration shown in Figure 8B

claim: Multi-angle light scattering analysis of S. rosetta CaMKII at ~200 μM reveals the existence of tetramers.
source: Multi-angle light scattering (MALS) analysis at much higher concentration (~200 μM) reveals the existence of tetramers (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by MALS shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2

claim: At 3 μM, the mass spectrum of S. rosetta CaMKII reveals mainly monomers and dimers, and a low abundance of tetramers.
source: At 3 μM, the mass spectrum reveals mainly monomers and dimers, and a low abundance of tetramers (Figure 8C).
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS shown in Figure 8C

claim: At 12 μM, the tetramer population of S. rosetta CaMKII increases, and a small population of hexamers emerges.
source: At 12 μM, the tetramer population increases, and a small population of hexamers also emerges.
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS shown in Figure 8C

claim: At 48 μM, the tetramer and hexamer populations of S. rosetta CaMKII increase further, and a population of octamers appears.
source: At 48 μM, the tetramer and hexamer populations increase further, and a population of octamers now appears.
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS shown in Figure 8C

claim: S. rosetta CaMKII undergoes subunit exchange readily without activation.
source: The variability in the stoichiometry of S. rosetta CaMKII suggests that it should undergo subunit exchange readily, without activation. We verified that this is the case by using the FRET-based exchange assay.
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET experiments

claim: Mixing donor and acceptor-labeled S. rosetta CaMKII without ATP or Ca2+/CaM results in a steady increase in FRET, consistent with subunit exchange.
source: Separate samples of full length S. rosetta CaMKII were labeled with donor (Alexa-488) and acceptor (Alexa-594) fluorophores, respectively, followed by mixing at ~5 μM final subunit concentration for each sample, without ATP or Ca2+/CaM. This results in a steady increase in FRET, consistent with subunit exchange (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by FRET experiments shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1

claim: Subunit exchange in S. rosetta CaMKII proceeds through dimer units.
source: We also monitored subunit exchange using native ESI-MS, which revealed that exchange proceeds through dimer units.
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS

claim: Mixing wild-type and linker-deleted S. rosetta CaMKII results in the generation of oligomers of variable stoichiometry containing both short and long forms in even stoichiometry.
source: For the exchange experiment, short (no linker) and long (wild type) forms of S. rosetta CaMKII are mixed at subunit concentrations of ~280 μM each and incubated for 15 min at 37°C. This was followed by buffer exchange into 1 M ammonium acetate (neutral pH) and the spectrum was acquired at a final concentration of ~10 μM (Figure 9A). This results in the generation of oligomers of variable stoichiometry, containing both short and long forms, in even stoichiometry (Figure 9B).
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS shown in Figure 9A-B

claim: The mass spectra reveal that subunit exchange in S. rosetta CaMKII occurs exclusively through exchange of dimers.
source: The mass spectra reveal that subunit exchange occurs exclusively through exchange of dimers.
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS

claim: Examination of the peaks corresponding to tetrameric assemblies of S. rosetta CaMKII shows that the mixed species are composed predominantly of even numbers of short and long subunits.
source: For example, examination of the peaks corresponding to dimeric and tetrameric assemblies shows that the mixed species are composed predominantly of even numbers of short and long subunits (data for tetrameric species are shown in Figure 9C).
evidence: Demonstrated by native ESI-MS shown in Figure 9C

claim: The interface that holds dimers together in all metazoan CaMKII hubs is very closely preserved in the S. rosetta hub.
source: Despite the striking dissimilarity in quaternary structure, the interface that holds dimers together in all metazoan CaMKII hubs is very closely preserved in the S. rosetta hub (Figure 10A–C), with helix D from one hub domain packed against the β-sheet of the adjacent domain.
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 10A-C

claim: When an interfacial region in the mouse tetradecameric hub assembly is superimposed on a corresponding region in the S. rosetta hub, the rms deviation in Cα positions is 0.35 Å over 22 residues.
source: When an interfacial region in the mouse tetradecameric hub assembly is superimposed on a corresponding region in the S. rosetta hub, the rms deviation in Cα positions is 0.35 Å over 22 residues.
evidence: Calculated from structural superposition

claim: The principal structural difference between a subunit in a closed-ring hub and one in the spiral S. rosetta hub is a rotation in the outer edge of the β-sheet with respect to the inner edge of the sheet and the α-helices.
source: The principal structural difference between a subunit in a closed-ring hub and one in the spiral S. rosetta hub is a rotation in the outer edge of the β-sheet with respect to the inner edge of the sheet and the α-helices (see Figure 10D).
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 10D

claim: A variation in the curvature of the β-sheet explains the variation in the assembly of all the hubs examined: the dodecameric and tetradecameric closed-ring hubs, the slightly ruptured left-handed spiral of the N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub and the open right-handed spiral of the S. rosetta hub.
source: A variation in the curvature of the β-sheet explains the variation in the assembly of all the hubs we have examined: the dodecameric and tetradecameric closed-ring hubs, the slightly ruptured left-handed spiral of the N. vectensis CaMKII-B hub and the open right-handed spiral of the S. rosetta hub (see Figure 10E for a schematic illustration of how a change in curvature of the β-sheet explains the transition from the dodecameric to the tetradecameric closed-ring forms).
evidence: Inferred from structural comparisons illustrated in Figure 10E

claim: The docking of a peptide between two subunits can force a change in the curvature of the β-sheet, thereby forcing a change in the oligomeric assembly.
source: Importantly, the docking of a peptide between two subunits can force a change in the curvature of the β-sheet, thereby forcing a change in the oligomeric assembly.
evidence: Inferred from structural and simulation data

claim: The lowest-frequency internal normal mode of a mouse CaMKII-α hub vertical dimer corresponds to a change in the curvature of the β-sheet.
source: The lowest-frequency internal normal mode corresponds to a change in the curvature of the β-sheet, such that one end of the β-sheet alters its distance from the helical layer, which stays relatively rigid.
evidence: Calculated using elastic network model

claim: If the structure of the mouse hub domain is displaced along the lowest-frequency normal mode, the changes in structure recapitulate the essential differences between the structures of the subunits in different hub assemblies, including the S. rosetta spiral.
source: If the structure of the mouse hub domain is displaced along this normal mode, then the changes in structure recapitulate the essential differences between the structures of the subunits in different hub assemblies, including the S. rosetta spiral, to a remarkable extent (Figure 11A).
evidence: Demonstrated by normal mode analysis shown in Figure 11A

claim: Low-frequency normal modes are indicative of low-energy deformations of the protein fold.
source: Low-frequency normal modes are indicative of low-energy deformations of the protein fold (Bahar and Rader, 2005), and so this suggests that the mammalian hub domains are intrinsically capable of the structural deformation that is required for the formation of an open spiral.
evidence: Supported by citation and inference from normal mode analysis

claim: Instantaneous structures sampled from molecular dynamics trajectories of a human decameric hub show that the structures of individual hub subunits undergo transient excursions in which the curvature of the β sheet is close to that seen in the S. rosetta structure.
source: Inspection of instantaneous structures sampled from these trajectories shows that the structures of individual hub subunits undergo transient excursions in which the curvature of the β sheet is close to that seen in the S. rosetta structure (Figure 11B).
evidence: Demonstrated by molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 11B

claim: The spiral geometry of a modeled human hub in the spiral configuration is stable in molecular dynamics trajectories, and the packing interactions at the hub interfaces remain intact.
source: We then initiated molecular dynamics trajectories from these modeled spiral structures (two replicates; 150 ns and 100 ns, respectively). The spiral geometry is stable in these trajectories, and the packing interactions at the hub interfaces remain intact (data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by molecular dynamics simulations

claim: The human sequence is consistent with the spiral architecture seen in the S. rosetta structure.
source: This indicates that the human sequence is consistent with the spiral architecture seen in the S. rosetta structure.
evidence: Inferred from molecular dynamics simulations

claim: The hub domain enables the CaMKII holoenzyme to switch between closed-ring dodecameric and tetradecameric states, and to potentially adopt ring-opened spiral configurations that can reversibly add and release dimer units.
source: We now show that the hub domain enables the CaMKII holoenzyme to switch between closed-ring dodecameric and tetradecameric states, and to potentially adopt ring-opened spiral configurations that can reversibly add and release dimer units to enable subunit exchange and interconversion between these states (Figure 12).
evidence: Concluded from all experimental and computational data, illustrated in Figure 12

claim: The CaM-binding element has an additional function beyond regulation of kinase activity, which is to dock at the interfaces between hub dimers and thereby distort the hub assembly.
source: Our data suggest that the CaM-binding element has an additional function, which is to dock at the interfaces between hub dimers, and thereby distort the hub assembly.
evidence: Inferred from structural and biochemical data

claim: The CaM-binding element induces the hub to transition from a closed-ring form to a ring-opened lock-washer configuration, which can release or capture dimer units.
source: Our data are consistent with the idea that the CaM-binding element induces the hub to transition from a closed-ring form to a ring-opened lock-washer configuration, which can release or capture dimer units.
evidence: Inferred from structural and biochemical data

claim: Subunit exchange in CaMKII need not involve complete disassembly and reassembly of the hub.
source: One attractive feature of this model, which is not directly tested here, is that subunit exchange need not involve complete disassembly and reassembly of the hub, which is likely to be a much less efficient process.
evidence: Proposed as a speculation based on the model

claim: The structures of CaMKII homologs from N. vectensis and S. rosetta provided crucial insight into the likely mechanism of subunit exchange.
source: The structures of CaMKII homologs from two distantly diverged organisms, the sea anemone N. vectensis and the choanoflagellate S. rosetta, provided crucial insight into the likely mechanism of subunit exchange.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion

claim: Activation-triggered subunit exchange provides a general mechanism to synchronize the functional states of a population of molecules, so that changes initiated by an input signal can spread from a small number of activated assemblies to many.
source: Activation-triggered subunit exchange provides a general mechanism to synchronize the functional states of a population of molecules, so that changes initiated by an input signal can spread from a small number of activated assemblies to many.
evidence: Proposed as a general principle
